Sunday. At lunch, Chinmay's father put down his glass. "Ankita's coaching fee is due, and the roof needs mending before the rains. You're the elder son, Chinmay. You'll manage." His mother nodded. Chinmay, back from a night shift, nodded too and reached for the rice.
Wednesday. He fell asleep on the bus and missed his stop by three stations. At his desk, he stared at the form for the exam he had wanted to take since March. The deadline was that Friday. He closed the tab.
Saturday. His younger sister Ankita found him on the terrace. "Bhaiya, you look so tired." "I'm fine." "You always say that." She sat beside him. Nobody had said it in months. He felt his throat tighten. "I'm not fine," he said, finally. "Not always."

qa.q: Which family member's coaching fee was due?
qa.a: Ankita's coaching fee was due.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when he closed the tab for the exam form?
qa.a: Chinmay felt worn out and quietly disappointed, giving up something he had wanted. His family duties left no room for it.

qa.q: What turning point on Saturday gave Chinmay a way forward?
qa.a: Ankita told him he looked tired and stayed beside him, and Chinmay finally said he was not always fine. Saying it aloud was the first step to being seen.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's father see his elder son's role?
qa.a: The father likely believes he is honouring a sincere duty and that Chinmay can manage. He may not have noticed the cost, since Chinmay nodded and said nothing.

grounding: An eldest son expected to sacrifice for everyone feels unseen when tired; the duty is sincere but costs more than one person can pay.

passage:
Noor, you said your family expects you to carry everything as the eldest daughter. Let me tell you about mine. I'm Akash, and at twenty-five I was the eldest son. My salary paid for my brother's fees, my mother's medical visits and the loan on the shop. Nobody was unkind. My father said thank you every month. But nobody asked me if I was tired.
One evening my Nani stopped me at the door. "Eat," she said, and put a bowl in my hands. "You look thinner than the rice." I sat down and cried, right there.
Next morning I told my mother, "I can pay for this half, but not all." She was quiet, then said, "I did not know you were so tired." It didn't fix everything, but it was the first time we talked about it.

qa.q: What did Akash's salary pay for at twenty-five?
qa.a: It paid for a brother's fees, a mother's medical visits and the loan on the shop.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when Nani put a bowl of food into Akash's hands?
qa.a: Akash felt exhausted and unseen, and being noticed at last released it in tears.

qa.q: What choice did Akash make the next morning?
qa.a: Akash told the mother that half could be paid but not all. That started an honest conversation about the tiredness.

qa.q: How did Akash's mother seem to feel on hearing that Akash was tired?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and perhaps sorry, since she said she had not known. Her quiet suggests she had not seen the cost of her son's giving.

grounding: An eldest child expected to sacrifice for everyone feels unseen until someone notices how tired he is; the duty was sincere but costly.

"Divyansh, the plumber is coming at nine, you'll wait, na?" Mummy said.
"Mummy, I have a client call at nine."
"Then move it. Lalit has college."
Lalit looked up from his cornflakes. "I can skip first period."
"No, no, your studies are important." Mummy turned back. "And Papa's pension papers, you'll take them to the bank on Saturday?"
"I did the electricity bill yesterday. I did Chachu's train tickets on Tuesday."
"Beta, you're the eldest. Who else will do it?"
Divyansh put his cup down. "I know. I want to help. But nobody asks if I'm tired."
The kitchen went quiet.
"Are you tired?" Lalit asked.
"Very."
Mummy looked at him properly for the first time that morning. "Why didn't you say?"
"I just did."

qa.q: What was Divyansh supposed to take to the bank on Saturday?
qa.a: Papa's pension papers.

qa.q: How did Divyansh seem to feel when he said nobody asks if he's tired?
qa.a: He felt unseen and worn out, still wanting to help but hurt that his tiredness had never been noticed.

qa.q: How could the family share the load more fairly?
qa.a: They could split tasks, letting Lalit wait for the plumber sometimes, and ask Divyansh what he can manage each week.

qa.q: What is it like for Mummy when she finally looks at Divyansh properly?
qa.a: She seems surprised and a little guilty, realising she had been treating her eldest as someone who never runs out.

grounding: Shows an eldest son expected to handle everything for the family feeling unseen and tired, even though his sense of duty is sincere.

passage:
I'm the eldest daughter, which in our house means I'm the one who remembers everything. Tanvir's school fees, Ammi's blood-pressure appointments, Nana's birthday, the gas cylinder.
Last Eid I cooked for twenty people after a week of night shifts at the call centre. Everyone praised the biryani. Nobody asked how I was. At eleven that night I washed the big pots alone and cried into the sink, quietly so Ammi wouldn't hear.
I don't regret helping. I love my family, and I'd do most of it again. But I realised that night that duty can be completely real and still be heavier than I can carry alone.
A week later I asked Tanvir to take over the gas bookings and the fee reminders. He said, "You should have told me years ago, Aparna Api." Maybe. I didn't know how.

qa.q: How many people did Aparna cook for last Eid?
qa.a: Twenty people.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling while washing the pots that night?
qa.a: She felt exhausted, unseen and sad, crying quietly after a day where everyone praised the food but nobody asked how she was.

qa.q: What small step helped Aparna, and why?
qa.a: Asking Tanvir to take over gas bookings and fee reminders shared the load without giving up her care for the family.

qa.q: How does Tanvir seem to see his sister's load now?
qa.a: He seems surprised and a bit regretful, wishing she had told him years ago so he could have helped.

grounding: Shows an eldest daughter whose sincere family duty costs more than she can pay, leaving her feeling unseen when tired.

Workplace wellbeing note, Tuesday.
Leela (25) booked a session after her manager noticed her crying at her desk. She is the eldest of three. Since her father's illness last year she has managed the household bills, her brother Kishore's college applications and her mother's hospital visits, while working full-time. She told me, "If I stop, everything stops. And nobody notices when I'm tired, only when something is late."
She spoke of her family with real love. She was not complaining about duty; she was describing a load that one person cannot keep carrying.
Together we listed the tasks and marked which ones Kishore, now nineteen, could take over. She agreed to talk to him this weekend. I gave her the service's number for evenings and booked a follow-up for next Tuesday.

qa.q: What does Leela manage since her father's illness?
qa.a: The household bills, her brother Kishore's college applications and her mother's hospital visits, while working full-time.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she said nobody notices when she's tired?
qa.a: She felt unseen and exhausted, as if her effort only mattered when something went wrong.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do next that could help?
qa.a: They listed the tasks with Leela, marked what Kishore could take over, gave her an evening support number and booked a follow-up.

qa.q: How might Kishore be affected when Leela talks to him?
qa.a: Kishore may be surprised by how much Leela has been carrying, and may feel glad or a bit guilty to take some of it on.

grounding: Shows an eldest daughter whose sincere sense of family duty leaves her unseen and overloaded, and the first steps to share it.

passage:
14 March, 11:40 pm
Divyansh's diary, since nobody else is listening today. Paid the electricity bill on the way home, picked up Papa's medicines, then Mummy called: Siddharth needs his laptop fee by Monday, and "you're the eldest, beta." I said yes before she finished. I always do. At dinner everyone talked about Siddharth's college fest. I nodded off sitting up and Papa laughed, "Office has made you lazy." I wanted to say I've been going since seven. I didn't. I do love them. I chose this. But tonight I'd give anything for one person to ask if I'm tired. Maybe I'll tell Siddharth tomorrow. He's the one who might actually hear it.

qa.q: What did Papa say when Divyansh nodded off at dinner?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "Office has made you lazy."

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling at the end of the day?
qa.a: Divyansh felt exhausted and unseen, still loving the family but longing for one person to ask about being tired.

qa.q: What could Divyansh say to Siddharth tomorrow?
qa.a: Divyansh could say plainly, "I've been running on empty. Can you take one errand this week?", which asks for help without blaming anyone.

qa.q: How might Papa see Divyansh nodding off at dinner?
qa.a: Papa sees only a sleepy Divyansh and turns it into a joke, not knowing the day began at seven with bills and errands.

grounding: Shows an eldest child who gives willingly to the family feeling exhausted and unseen when nobody notices the cost.
